title: AI Disclosure — EPPS 6356 Assignment 4 (Chart Hackathon)
text:
Per the assignment rule “AI is allowed, with disclosure. For each chart, record the tool, model and version, date, and full prompts, plus two or three sentences on what you had to fix in the AI’s output.”
Each team member documents their own charts below.



Author: Shao-Kang (Eric) Huang Tool: Claude (Anthropic), model claude-opus-5, used in the Claude desktop app Date: 5 October 2026 Files produced: assignments/Chart4.R, R/theme.R, data/hpi_chart4_means.rds, output/chart4_continent_means.png


The conversation was held in Traditional Chinese. The prompts that produced the committed code are reproduced below with English translations.


接著幫我依照他的風格完成第四張圖 (Now complete the fourth chart for me, following her style.)

Context supplied to the model beforehand: the assignment PDF, the teammate’s published page https://nedretsencavus.github.io/portfolio/assignments/assign04.html, and read access to this repository after it was cloned locally — in particular assignments/Chart3.R, assignments/assign04.qmd, and data/hpi_clean.csv.

幫我看一下 (Take a look at this for me.) — sent with the first rendered PNG, which asked the model to review the output against the other three charts.






The y-axis title came out horizontal. theme_hackathon() re-declares axis.title.y through %+replace% without an angle, so the angle resets to 0, the title is printed flat at the far left, and the panel is squeezed. I caught this when I compared the first render against Chart 1, where the same fix (element_text(angle = 90, vjust = 2, margin = margin(r = 10))) already appears. The model had not carried that line over; it was added in commit 07f074f.
The first draft of the commit would have touched the whole repository. Because the clone is on a Windows machine, every text file in the repo showed as modified on line endings alone (13,521 insertions / 13,527 deletions across 52 files, all whitespace). I staged only the four new paths instead of using git add -A, so the commit history stays readable.
source("R/theme.R") pointed at a file that was not in the repository. Chart1.R and Chart3.R both call it, but the theme existed only inside the setup chunk of assign04.qmd, so those two scripts failed from a clean R session. I had the palettes and theme_hackathon() extracted into R/theme.R and verified that all four chart scripts now run from the project root, which is what the checklist item “code runs from a clean R session using only the repo contents” requires.





Sorting the continents by mean HPI rather than alphabetically, so the chart answers its own title.
Printing n = inside each column. Oceania’s mean rests on four countries and Asia’s on seventeen; without the counts the five columns read as equally reliable.
Stating the mean is unweighted in the subtitle, since Chart 1 uses a population-weighted mean and the two numbers would otherwise appear to disagree.






(Nedret: please add your tool, model, date, prompts and fixes here. If a chart was written without AI assistance, say so explicitly — the rule asks for disclosure either way.)



Tool: ChatGPT
Model: GPT-5.6 Sol
Date: October 6, 2026


Prompt 1:
“Help me redesign Chart 3 so that the Top 20 and Bottom 20 HPI countries are shown on one continuous horizontal scale rather than in separate panels. The redesign should improve direct comparison, remain consistent with the team’s shared theme and color palette, and still satisfy the assignment requirement of comparing one variable across many items.”
Prompt 2:
“Help me rework the Chart 3 code so that countries are ranked by HPI, Top 20 and Bottom 20 are distinguished with the shared color-blind-safe palette, exact HPI values are labeled directly, and the chart includes a data-driven takeaway title and a clear separator between the two groups.”
Prompt 3:
“Rewrite the Chart 3 implementation and analytical takeaway so that they accurately explain the redesigned continuous ranking, justify the visualization choices using comparison and perceptual clarity, and avoid making claims that are not directly supported by the chart.”



The initial AI-generated approach was revised to match the actual structure of the team repository, the shared theme.R file, and the variables available in hpi_chart3.rds. The final redesign replaced the earlier faceted layout with a single continuous ranked bar chart, used the project’s existing color-blind-safe palette, calculated the headline gap directly from the data, and adjusted file paths so the chart rendered correctly within the Quarto site. The analytical text was also revised to focus only on patterns directly supported by the visualization and dataset.

title: Mapping Discretionary Discipline in Texas School Districts
text:
This page maps the team project data: Texas Education Agency (TEA) district discipline counts, joined to U.S. Census Bureau school-district boundaries. Every map is a rate, a share or a count. Rates and shares are drawn as filled areas (choropleths) and counts as sized symbols, so raw counts are never shown as fill and the denominator is never left out (Cairo 2019, How Charts Lie). The static maps use the Albers equal-area projection (EPSG:5070), because a choropleth asks readers to compare areas (Lovelace, Nowosad, and Muenchow, Geocomputation with R, ch. 2 and 9).
Mapped measure. Discretionary removals per 100 enrolled students = (in-school suspension actions + out-of-school suspension actions + discretionary DAEP placement actions) ÷ cumulative year-end enrollment × 100. These come from TEA section B (“Discipline data”, action counts) and section A (“Cumulative year end enrollment”). TEA masks small values for student privacy (“<10”, “<20”, …), and those cells are treated as missing, not zero. TEA prints no row when a category is zero, so absent rows count as 0.
Code
library(tidyverse); library(sf); library(tmap); library(patchwork)

# Files written by R/prepare_map_data.R
files <- c(disc  = "data/tea_discipline_district.csv",
           xwalk = "data/ccd_crosswalk_tx.csv",
           bnd   = "data/tx_school_districts.rds")
if (any(!file.exists(files))) {
  stop("Missing: ", paste(files[!file.exists(files)], collapse = ", "),
       ". Run R/prepare_map_data.R first.")
}

disc <- read_csv(files[["disc"]], show_col_types = FALSE,
                 col_types = cols(year = col_character(), cdn = col_character(),
                                  district_name = col_character(),
                                  charter_status = col_character(), .default = col_double()))
xwalk <- read_csv(files[["xwalk"]], col_types = cols(.default = col_character()))
districts <- readRDS(files[["bnd"]])          # sf, stored in EPSG:4326

latest_year <- max(disc$year)                 # e.g., "2023-24"
pct <- function(p) scales::percent(p, accuracy = 1)

title: Mapping Discretionary Discipline in Texas School Districts
text:
1. Join and check
TEA identifies districts by a 6-digit county-district number (CDN). Census boundaries use the 7-digit NCES LEAID (GEOID). The NCES Common Core of Data directory links the two. The data-preparation script already fixes what can be fixed: it pads CDNs back to six digits when spreadsheet software drops leading zeros or adds apostrophes.


Code
disc_latest <- disc |>
  filter(year == latest_year) |>
  left_join(xwalk, by = "cdn")                # CDN -> GEOID

districts_map <- districts |>
  left_join(disc_latest, by = "geoid") |>
  st_transform("EPSG:5070")                   # Albers equal-area for static maps

# TEA districts with no matching boundary
unmatched <- disc_latest |>
  anti_join(st_drop_geometry(districts), by = "geoid") |>
  mutate(reason = if_else(is.na(geoid),
                          "No NCES LEAID in the CCD crosswalk",
                          "LEAID has no Census boundary polygon")) |>
  select(cdn, district_name, charter_status, enrolled, reason) |>
  arrange(reason, district_name)

print(unmatched, n = Inf)

title: Mapping Discretionary Discipline in Texas School Districts
text:
2. Projection comparison


Code
# Latitude of a point inside each district (computed in a projected CRS, as sf advises)
lat <- districts |> st_geometry() |> st_transform(5070) |>
  st_point_on_surface() |> st_transform(4326) |> st_coordinates()

tx2 <- districts |>
  mutate(hl = case_when(lat[, "Y"] >= 34 ~ "Panhandle (north of 34°N)",
                        lat[, "Y"] <= 27 ~ "South Texas (south of 27°N)",
                        .default = "Other"))

panel <- function(crs) ggplot(st_transform(tx2, crs)) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = hl), colour = NA) + labs(title = crs) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Panhandle (north of 34°N)" = "#1f4e79",
                               "South Texas (south of 27°N)" = "#c0504d",
                               Other = "grey85"), guide = "none") +
  theme_void(base_size = 11)

c("EPSG:4326", "EPSG:3857", "EPSG:5070") |> map(panel) |> wrap_plots(nrow = 1) +
  plot_annotation(
    title = "The same Texas school districts in three coordinate reference systems",
    subtitle = "Blue: Panhandle districts (north of 34°N). Red: South Texas districts (south of 27°N).",
    caption = "Boundaries: U.S. Census Bureau cartographic school districts (2023) via tigris.")









In EPSG:4326, ggplot draws longitude and latitude as a flat grid scaled to Texas’s middle latitude. Meridians therefore stay parallel, so east–west distances come out slightly too wide in the Panhandle and too narrow in South Texas. Web Mercator (EPSG:3857) is worse: it inflates every area by the square of the secant of latitude, about 1.24× at 26°N but 1.53× at 36°N, so Panhandle districts look roughly a quarter larger than South Texas districts of the same size. I would publish the Albers equal-area version (EPSG:5070), because a choropleth asks readers to compare colored areas, and only an equal-area projection keeps each district’s ink in proportion to the land it covers.

# Numbers used in the paragraph below
x <- na.omit(districts_map$disc_rate)
brks <- map(set_names(names(class_titles)),
            \(s) classInt::classIntervals(x, n = 5, style = s)$brks)

top_start <- map_dbl(brks, \(b) b[length(b) - 1])


With equal intervals, 3% of districts fall in the darkest class, because the rates are right-skewed (mean 15.2 vs. median 15.1 per 100 students); most of the state shares one or two pale colors and the map mainly flags outliers. Quantile classes put about 20% of districts in each class by design. That spreads color across the state, but the darkest class starts at 20.3, so districts with nearly the same rate on either side of a break can look very different. Jenks breaks follow gaps in the data and start the darkest class at 24.5 (8% of districts), a middle ground between the other two. I would publish the quantile map: readers rank colors, and equal-count classes give every color the same meaning (one fifth of districts), as long as the legend says the classes are quintiles.

text:
For Assignment 7 our team built a reactive R Shiny application that displays three charts from Andrew Abela’s Chart Suggestions: A Thought-Starter (2006), using the 2026 Happy Planet Index (HPI) public data set for 2006–2025. All three charts read from a single reactive() data set, so a change to the year or the regions updates every chart at once. Drag a box on the scatter chart to highlight those countries in the bubble chart and rank them in the bar chart, hover over a bubble for exact values, or press play under the year slider to animate 2006–2025.

The Three Charts









Abela no.
Chart
What it shows
Why this encoding




9
Scatter chart
Any two of five variables (GDP per capita, wellbeing, life expectancy, ecological footprint, HPI score), coloured by World Bank region
Both quantities are encoded as position along a common scale, the most accurately judged elementary task (Cleveland & McGill 1984); it is the hypothesis-forming view (Ware 2012)


18
Bubble chart
GDP per capita (log scale) against HPI score; bubble area shows population or ecological footprint
Area is the least accurate channel, so it carries only the contextual third variable; area, not radius, is proportional to the value (Tufte 2001; Cairo 2019)


3
Bar chart (our choice)
Countries ranked by HPI score, with the world median as a reference line
The HPI is one value per country across more than 130 countries, Abela’s case of comparison among many items; bars start at zero so differences are not exaggerated (Cairo 2019)



The charts are linked views: countries brushed on Chart 9 stay coloured on Chart 18 while the rest fade, and Chart 3 ranks exactly that selection. Every chart has a message title computed from the data, axis titles with units, a source note, and the colour-blind-safe Okabe–Ito palette.

title: Chart Producing Hackathon: Visualizing the Happy Planet Index
text:
For Assignment 4 in Dr. Karl Ho’s EPPS 6356 Data Visualization course, our objective was to operationalize Andrew Abela’s Chart Thought-Starter taxonomy using empirical data from the 2024 Happy Planet Index (HPI). The assignment required building a fully reproducible, self-contained repository in R, deploying the resulting figures to GitHub Pages, and demonstrating clear collaborative ownership.
As team coordinator, I designed the foundation for the team before any visualization code was drafted. In line with Dr. Ho’s recommendation to settle design foundations early, I initialized the remote GitHub repository. I then developed, debugged, and refined Charts 1, 2, and 3, and established the branch architecture to delegate Chart 4 to my teammates.
This report documents the architectural setup, mathematical boundaries, visual design theories, debugging challenges, and substantive findings that went into completing this sprint. All figures share a unified styling system, adhere to Edward Tufte’s data-ink maximization, utilize color-blind safe palettes (Okabe & Ito 2008), and encode comparisons along common spatial baselines (Cleveland & McGill 1984).

Analytical Takeaway

The Population Weighting Effect: Looking strictly at national averages, Latin American nations post the highest individual HPI scores globally. However, when weighting by population, Europe leads all continents with a score of 49.4 across roughly 750 million people. The Americas place second at 46.7; while countries like Costa Rica (62.1) and Colombia (60.2) demonstrate world-class efficiency, the region’s aggregate score is pulled down by the demographic mass and heavy ecological footprint of the United States (37.4 across 333 million people).
Demographic Mass vs. Sustainable Return: Asia spans the largest horizontal share of the chart—representing nearly 4 billion people in this sample—yet achieves an intermediate efficiency score of 44.9. Oceania maintains a solid 46.0, though its demographic footprint is a narrow sliver on the far right (roughly 32 million people). Africa records the lowest regional weighted score at 36.6 across roughly 880 million people, constrained primarily by systemic deficits in life expectancy and basic public health infrastructure rather than resource overconsumption.

Analytical Takeaway

The Income–Footprint Decoupling: The inline pressure bars visually expose that high national wealth does not translate into sustainable efficiency. High-income economies like Luxembourg ($116,300 GDP pc) and Qatar ($93,500 GDP pc) achieve high life expectancy (82.6 and 79.3 years), but generate massive ecological footprints (12.80 and 14.30 gha/capita). These resource demands stretch their pressure bars to the maximum and drag their overall HPI scores down to 33.5 and 22.6.
High Efficiency at Low Cost: Middle- and low-income economies achieve comparable health and happiness outcomes at a fraction of the ecological throughput. Costa Rica ($20,300 GDP pc) and Vanuatu ($3,150 GDP pc) deliver life expectancies of 80.3 and 70.5 years with subjective wellbeing at 7.0/10, all while keeping footprints under 2.7 gha/capita. Their efficiency bars fill nearly two-thirds of the cell, demonstrating that human development does not require exponential carbon consumption.
Two Routes to Low Scores: The bottom rows highlight two distinct failure mechanisms. In the United States (HPI 37.4) and Qatar (HPI 22.6), low efficiency stems from excessive consumption (footprints of 7.80 and 14.30 gha). In the Central African Republic (HPI 21.1), the low score is driven by acute humanitarian hardship—life expectancy drops to 53.9 years and wellbeing falls to 3.5, even though its footprint is minimal at 1.45 gha/capita.

text:
Analytical Takeaway

Large spread across the ranking: The continuous ordering reveals a substantial gap between the highest- and lowest-ranked countries. Costa Rica has the highest HPI score at 62.1, while the Central African Republic has the lowest score at 21.1, producing a difference of 41.0 points. Displaying all 40 countries on one common scale makes this overall spread immediately visible and easier to compare than if the two cohorts were shown in separate panels.
Regional concentration among the highest-ranked countries: Many of the highest HPI scores are concentrated in Latin America and the Caribbean. Costa Rica, Colombia, Ecuador, Panama, Jamaica, Guatemala, Honduras, Nicaragua, Peru, Mexico, and the Dominican Republic all appear in the Top 20. However, the Top 20 is not regionally uniform, as countries such as Switzerland, Norway, Finland, Spain, Japan, Vietnam, and the Philippines also rank highly.
The Bottom 20 is geographically diverse: The lower end of the ranking includes countries from Africa, Europe, Asia, the Americas, and the Middle East. Examples include Senegal, Ghana, Kenya, Estonia, Bulgaria, Egypt, Uganda, the United States, Tanzania, Saudi Arabia, Ethiopia, Nigeria, Luxembourg, the United Arab Emirates, South Africa, Sierra Leone, Mongolia, Zimbabwe, Qatar, and the Central African Republic. This indicates that low HPI scores are not confined to a single region.
The visualization emphasizes comparison rather than explanation: Chart 3 shows how countries differ in HPI score, but it does not by itself explain why those differences occur. Variables such as life expectancy, wellbeing, ecological footprint, and GDP per capita are present in the dataset, but they are not encoded in this chart. Therefore, the chart should be interpreted as a ranked comparison of HPI outcomes rather than as evidence of causal relationships.

section: Chart 4: Column Chart of Continental Means
text:
Chart 4: Column Chart of Continental Means

Implementation (Comparison: One Variable across a Few Items)
Chart 4 completes the Abela comparison branch at its coarsest grain: one variable (the Happy Planet Index) across a few items (the five continents). Continents are ordered by mean HPI with forcats::fct_reorder() rather than alphabetically, so the ranking is read from position along a common baseline (Cleveland & McGill 1984) instead of recovered by scanning labels. The mean here is unweighted, which distinguishes it from the population-weighted mean in Chart 1; the two figures are not interchangeable and the subtitle says so. Because a continental mean conceals how many countries it averages — four for Oceania against seventeen for Asia — the count is printed inside each column rather than relegated to a footnote.


Render Chart 4: geom_col() Continental Means with Embedded Counts
df_chart4 <- hpi_clean %>%
  group_by(continent) %>%
  summarise(
    mean_hpi = mean(hpi, na.rm = TRUE),
    n        = dplyr::n(),
    .groups  = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(continent_ordered = fct_reorder(continent, mean_hpi, .desc = TRUE))

p4 <- ggplot(df_chart4, aes(x = continent_ordered, y = mean_hpi, fill = continent)) +
  geom_col(
    width = 0.68,
    show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = sprintf("%.1f", mean_hpi)),
    vjust = -0.55,
    size = 3.6,
    fontface = "bold",
    color = "#222222"
  ) +
  geom_text(
    aes(y = 1.8, label = paste0("n = ", n)),
    size = 2.9,
    color = "#FFFFFF",
    fontface = "bold"
  ) +
  scale_fill_continent() +
  scale_x_discrete(name = "Continent") +
  scale_y_continuous(
    name   = "Mean Happy Planet Index Score (0-100 Scale)",
    limits = c(0, 62),
    breaks = seq(0, 60, by = 10),
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.02))
  ) +
  labs(
    title    = "The Americas Convert Resources into Wellbeing More Efficiently Than Any Other Continent",
    subtitle = "Unweighted mean Happy Planet Index of the countries in each continent; n gives the number of countries behind each column.",
    caption  = "Source: Happy Planet Index (2024 Edition) | EPPS 6356 Hackathon"
  ) +
  theme_hackathon(legend_pos = "none") +
  theme(
    # theme_hackathon() re-declares axis.title.y through %+replace% without an
    # angle, which prints the title flat and squeezes the panel; the same fix
    # is applied in Chart 1.
    axis.title.y = element_text(angle = 90, vjust = 2, margin = margin(r = 10))
  )

p4











Analytical Takeaway

The Americas lead on efficiency, not on income. At a mean of 53.5 across sixteen countries, the Americas sit roughly six points above Oceania (49.7) and nearly six above Europe (47.9), despite a lower average GDP per capita than Europe. This is the HPI’s central claim made visible at continental scale: the index rewards converting resources into long, satisfying lives, not accumulating resources.
Africa’s position is a footprint artefact as much as a wellbeing one. Africa’s mean of 36.3 is the lowest of the five, but the cohort spreads from 21.1 to 47.6 — a range wider than the gap between the top two continents. Reading the column as a statement about “Africa” rather than about its mean would be exactly the error the embedded counts are there to resist.
Oceania’s column is the least reliable and says so. Four countries stand behind a mean of 49.7, against seventeen behind Asia’s 43.3. Printing n inside the bar keeps that asymmetry in the reader’s eye at the moment of comparison; without it, five columns of identical construction imply five estimates of identical precision.
Sorting is the analysis. Ordering by mean rather than alphabetically turns the ranking into a single left-to-right read. Wickham (2010) names alphabetical ordering of categorical variables as a common and avoidable fault, after Wainer’s “Alabama first!”; here, sorting is what allows the title’s claim to be verified by looking.

Technical Troubleshooting & Debugging Log
During development, several technical issues required hands-on troubleshooting to keep the project moving:

Package Installation & System Permissions: Running install.packages("dplyr", "tidyr", ...) initially threw directory errors because missing c() wrappers caused R to misinterpret package names as local paths and download repositories. In addition, Windows compilation prompts for Rtools appeared. I resolved this by setting options(pkgType = "binary") to pull pre-compiled binaries, avoiding unnecessary local compiler builds.
Quarto Path Resolution: Early preview runs failed with cannot open the connection on source("R/theme.R") because the file was saved in an external folder. I wrote an inline script generator to save R/theme.R directly into the project root, satisfying the self-contained repository requirement.
YAML Parser Crashes: Quarto threw readBlockMapping2 errors due to a merged title/subtitle line and non-breaking space characters (\u00A0) in the YAML header. I rebuilt the front matter with standard two-space indentation and dedicated lines for every key.
Table Cell Clipping: The gt table’s right-aligned currency columns were getting clipped during headless rendering in Chrome. Setting fixed pixel widths on every column via cols_width() resolved the overflow.

For all these errors I asked Gemini- Flash Extended model. I gave my code and the warning error I got in the console to Gemini and asked why it happpened, and how I could fix it.

EPPS 6356 Data Visualization, Fall 2026 — Nedret Sen Cavus





One row of the map is one Texas public school district (local education agency) in one school year. The static maps show the latest year (2023–24); the dashboard covers 2018–19 to 2023–24.
Boundaries come from the U.S. Census Bureau cartographic (1:500k) school-district files for 2023, read with tigris::school_districts(state = "TX", cb = TRUE, year = 2023). Unified districts are the main layer; elementary and secondary districts are added where the Census reports them for Texas.
Join key. TEA identifies districts by a 6-digit county-district number (CDN). Census polygons use the 7-digit NCES LEAID (GEOID). The NCES Common Core of Data LEA directory (2022) links the two: its state_leaid (e.g., TX-057905) carries the CDN and its leaid equals the Census GEOID. The join is TEA CDN → CCD crosswalk → Census GEOID. Open-enrollment charter schools have no geographic boundary, so they remain unmatched by design; maps.qmd lists them with anti_join().

Storage: EPSG:4326 (WGS 84 longitude/latitude). It is the neutral exchange format: tigris boundaries are reprojected to it once and saved, so every later step starts from the same coordinates.
Static maps: EPSG:5070 (NAD83 / Conus Albers equal-area). The assignment default for the contiguous U.S.; it keeps district areas proportional to land area, which a choropleth needs because readers compare colored areas.

Colour scale: quantile (5 classes) vs. continuous.
Minimum denominator: rates computed from fewer students than the threshold are hidden (grey), so noisy small-group rates are not overinterpreted (Hullman 2020). Each measure is compared with its own denominator (all, Black, or White students).

One shared reactive() holds the filtered sf data. It feeds the Leaflet map (redrawn with leafletProxy()), three value boxes (districts shown, districts without a rate, median of the selected measure), and a companion top-10 dot plot drawn on a common scale from zero (Cleveland and McGill 1984).
